reviews.one_line_contribution: Inside a name-swapping wrapper on ALFWorld it plants a per-kitchen procedure binding (which of two look-alike appliances actually heats/cools/cleans) and independently switches whether a wrong choice answers back ('Nothing happens') or silently consumes the step, to show that a 60-token run-time-probe rule substitutes for a retriever when the environment gives a signal, while a ~900-token observation-keyed table compiled from the same bank substitutes for it when the environment gives none.
reviews.closest_prior_work: Closest verified: MEMENTO, arXiv:2505.16348 ('Embodied Agents Meet Personalization: Investigating Challenges and Solutions Through the Lens of Memory Utilization', 2025-05-22, 12 cites; verified with `s2cli.py paper 2505.16348`, S2 channel). It plants exactly this proposal's independent variable — instance-specific bindings in an embodied household environment that are recoverable only from stored episodes (user-specific object semantics and routines) — and it already separates memory retrieval from memory application, which is the split this proposal advertises as new relative to Mem2ActBench. It does not threaten the core: it never scores a retriever against a compiled static artifact built from the same experience at matched tokens, and it never manipulates whether the binding can be probed before committing, which is this proposal's actual axis. Second threat, verified: SGR-Bench arXiv:2605.22219 (2026-05-21) — state-gated retrieval is precisely the 'testable' regime (state must be established, and the site tells you when it is wrong); it is a benchmark of failures, not a manipulation, and has no compiled-vs-retrieved arms. A third body of work the proposal never engages bounds two of its predictions rather than its headline: context-vs-parametric knowledge conflict (arXiv:2506.06485 'What Is Seen Cannot Be Unseen', returned by my --recent query on the HF channel; arXiv:2604.22193, 2026-04-24, same query). P1 ('does the reader keep its prior over a corrected exemplar?') and P3 ('will the reader prefer a retrieved trajectory's appliance name to its prior?') are context-memory conflict questions in agent clothing, and that literature already reports readers falling back on internal knowledge under conflict. That makes P1's and P3's mechanism less new than the proposal claims, though the testable/untestable interaction on top of it is not preempted.
reviews.strongest_objection: The headline interaction is half stipulated, and the proposal says so itself: 'under untestable the rule is inert by construction', and D(S1, untestable) within +-8 of D(S0, untestable) is filed as a 'construction check, reported not scored'. So the 'only when untestable' claim decomposes into (a) a wrapper property the authors built, not a finding, and (b) three reader-capability facts about one 32B model — can it execute a two-branch probe rule, can it route a 30-row observation-keyed table to the right row, will it override 'microwave heats' when a retrieved trajectory says stoveburner. An AC will say: you constructed an environment in which a rule cannot possibly fire, then reported that the rule does not fire. Compounding this, the binding is not a generic instance-specific binding but a deliberate collision with the reader's parametric prior, and there is no binding level that avoids that collision (e.g. which of two identically-named cabinets is the working one), so every headline number is confounded with knowledge-conflict strength and may not survive a backbone change — a limitation the Risk section concedes but the design does not address. Finally the framing is inconsistent with its own P4: if the compiled table matches retrieval under untestable, the paper's result is 'you never need a retriever, compile a keyed table', which is the opposite of the title's 'A Query Is Needed Only for Untestable Bindings'; the hypothesis rescues this only by redefining 'per-instance lookup' to include a cached static table, which is exactly not a query.
reviews.what_would_fix_it: 1) Add a binding level that does not fight the parametric prior (two same-named receptacles, or an arbitrary tag, rather than microwave<->stoveburner), so P1/P3 measure binding transfer rather than knowledge-conflict strength; report the swap penalty at both levels. 2) Run the third regime the proposal excludes (undetectable but reversible) with the 30-token redundancy rule, so that the 'best static alternative' retrieval is scored against is measured rather than fixed by the wrapper's design; as written, the untestable wrapper is built to defeat every cheap static artifact except enumeration, which is what P4 then tests. 3) Fix P6: make W- carry the opposite binding deterministically instead of a random other-kitchen item that is correct about half the time under complementary assignments, which halves the estimand against a 12-point margin and biases the test toward falsification. 4) Define the 12-20 band for the P1 gate; as written, continuation is undefined in that band, and the entailment check is right that D(S0)-D(S3) collapses algebraically to a single swapped-game contrast. 5) Put the table's row count in the design (30 -> 100 -> 300 rows by merging kitchens or importing bindings) — the table-vs-query crossover lives exactly where the proposal declines to look, and P4 without it reads as an artifact of a benchmark with ~30 kitchens. 6) Retitle to what P4 actually claims. Dropping the type-agnostic T0/T1 or one seed pays for 1-3 within the same ~11.5 h budget.
reviews.missing_baseline: The redundancy static rule under untestable — a ~30-token 'do the procedure step at both candidate appliances' instruction on top of static3. The proposal names it and refuses it, on the grounds that the untestable wrapper makes later attempts on either appliance return the success string without effect. That is a wrapper decision, not a property of silent real-world failures (silent API/UI failures are frequently retry-safe), and it means the 'best static arm' that every retrieval residual is reported against is chosen by construction rather than measured, which is a direct violation of the brief's binding rule that retrieval be scored against the best static alternative built from the same experience. It is also far cheaper than the ~900-token table, so if it works the paper's cost story changes sign. Secondary omissions a reviewer will also ask for: a non-prior-conflicting binding level (see above), and a second backbone restricted to P2 and P4, since both are reader-capability operations rather than environment properties.
reviews.preprint_collision: No verified collision. My queries, all answered by channel (a), the s2cli literature command (S2+HF); WebSearch was unavailable in this session and was not used. (1) mechanism, unrestricted: 'instance-specific bindings retrieved experience versus compiled static prompt LLM agent' -> nothing on the mechanism (2607.14159 MemoHarness, 2606.04536 parametric memory, 2511.05931 SAGE, 2310.02107 PRoMPTd). (2) mechanism, --recent: 'when is retrieval necessary agent memory environment feedback probe versus stored trajectory binding' -> 2607.10608 Compliance Trap, 2607.24368 InMind, 2606.19911 MATM, 2602.16313 MemoryArena, 2608.02508 RoMeRL; none manipulates feedback testability or compares compiled artifacts with a retriever. (3) closest named method: 'Agent Workflow Memory induce reusable workflows from trajectories' -> AWM itself was NOT returned (2608.10509 MAP-Graph, 2607.20999 WML, 2608.25570 KOPE, 2607.01709 COMFYCLAW); the proposal's Q9 hit the same wall, so its claim that AWM is 'the nearest compiled form' with no run-time probe is unverified on both sides — it cites no arXiv id for AWM and I could not verify one. (4) --recent, silent-failure framing -> 2606.22936, 2607.07405, 2605.08747, 2607.13083; diagnostic work only, no retrieval-vs-compiled contrast. (5) --recent, 'compiled lookup table in prompt versus top-k retrieval matched tokens agent success cost' -> 2608.22695 Enrich-Retrieve-Rank (in-context routing collapses as a registry grows — the closest thing to a prior on P4, and it points against the table at scale), 2608.14943 Skill Blocks (caching-correct comparison of pre-load vs on-demand skill loading, the nearest cost-side analogue), 2603.13017; none plants bindings. (6) home vocabulary, no agent/memory words: 'latent task variable must be inferred from feedback versus given in demonstrations in-context learning exploration' -> 2605.26350 'When Correct Demonstrations Hurt', 2309.07900, 2305.16985; nothing on run-time testability. (7) 'context versus parametric knowledge conflict...' --recent -> 2506.06485, 2604.22193, 2503.15888. Verification of the ids the proposal's novelty argument rests on, all via `s2cli.py paper` (S2): 2606.22936 VERIFIED (2026-06-22, 7 cites, premature commitment, diagnostic — the proposal characterizes it correctly); 2605.22219 VERIFIED (SGR-Bench, 100 tasks); 2601.19935 VERIFIED (Mem2ActBench, ACL, 26 cites); 2602.08316 VERIFIED (SWE-ContextBench); 2406.14596 VERIFIED (ICAL, NeurIPS, 61 cites); 2305.09731 VERIFIED (task recognition vs task learning, ACL, 190 cites). Not verified: AWM (no id given, not returned by either channel). Judging the proposal's own check: it is better than most in this round — five classed queries with channels and ids, including a genuine home-vocabulary query stripped of agent/memory words, as the brief requires. Two real gaps: the closest-named-method query failed and was not retried by id, and the check never searched the context-vs-parametric knowledge-conflict literature, which is the actual home literature for P1 and P3 and which supplies a prior (readers resist overriding internal knowledge) that the proposal treats as an open question. The novelty card itself is near-useless here — its top hits are scene-text retrieval (2506.10609) and structured-metadata retrieval (2606.30473), i.e. embedding-similarity noise on the word 'scene' and 'binding' — so the novelty judgement rests on my queries and on MEMENTO, which the card missed entirely.
